title: What is the Singleton pattern, and how do you write a thread-safe, lazily initialized implementation (eager, lazy, synchronized, double-checked locking with volatile, Bill Pugh holder, enum)?
shortTitle: What is the Singleton pattern and how to write a thread-safe lazy implementation
keyPoints: Lazy initialization builds the instance only on first use, saving resources when construction is expensive.
Eager initialization is thread-safe via class loading but wastes resources if the instance is never used.
Synchronized getter is lazy and correct but locks every call, even after the instance exists.
Double-checked locking checks null without a lock, then locks and checks again; requires volatile to prevent partial construction.
Bill Pugh holder uses a private static inner class; the JVM's class-initialization guarantee makes it lazy and thread-safe with no explicit synchronization.
Enum singleton is immune to serialization, reflection, and cloning; Effective Java calls it the best approach.

s1_definition.oneliner: A lazy thread-safe Singleton builds the single instance only on first use, safely under concurrency, and the cleanest ways are the Bill Pugh holder idiom and the enum.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Singleton** – guarantees one instance for the entire application with a single access point.
- **Lazy initialization** – creates the instance only on first use, important when construction is expensive.
- **Thread safety** – concurrent threads must not be able to create two instances.
- **Bill Pugh holder** – lazy + safe via JVM class-initialization guarantee, no synchronization needed.
- **Enum singleton** – most robust: immune to serialization, reflection, and cloning by JVM design.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps one shared audit ledger for the whole bank. There must never be two ledgers, because two ledgers could record conflicting versions of the same transaction. The bank also prefers to open this ledger only when the first transaction actually needs it, and when dozens of tellers reach for it at the same second, exactly one ledger must be created and shared.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Singleton Thread-Safety Approaches
  ──────────────────────────────────

  Eager:       class load ──▶ INSTANCE created (always)
  Sync getter: every call ──▶ LOCK ──▶ null check ──▶ create/return
  DCL:         null check ──▶ null? LOCK ──▶ check again ──▶ create
                              not null? ──▶ return (fast)
  Bill Pugh:   getInstance() ──▶ touch Holder class
                                  ──▶ JVM loads once ──▶ create
  Enum:        INSTANCE ──▶ JVM guarantees one
                          ──▶ immune to clone/serial/reflect

  Recommended:
  ┌────────────┬───────────────────────┐
  │ Enum       │ Default choice        │
  │ Bill Pugh  │ When extending a class│
  └────────────┴───────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Singleton pattern guarantees one instance for the whole application. A thread-safe, lazily initialised Singleton creates that instance only on first use while preventing concurrent threads from creating duplicates.

Rajesh walks through the options from weakest to strongest. Eager initialization is thread-safe but not lazy. The synchronized getter is lazy but locks every call. Double-checked locking locks only on first creation but requires `volatile` to prevent another thread from seeing a partially-constructed object.

The two Rajesh prefers are the Bill Pugh holder and the enum. Bill Pugh uses a private static inner class that the JVM loads only when `getInstance()` touches it, giving lazy, thread-safe creation with no `synchronized` or `volatile`. The enum declares a single constant that the JVM guarantees is one instance, immune to serialization, reflection, and cloning, which is why Effective Java recommends it.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj uses the enum for the shared rate registry and the Bill Pugh holder for the audit ledger that needs special constructor logic. He also remembers that a JVM Singleton is one per JVM, not one per cluster.

Remember one sentence: use the enum for free safety against serialization, reflection, and cloning, and the Bill Pugh holder when you need lazy class-based construction with no explicit synchronization.
